title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
Cline deployed an AI agent to automatically triage GitHub issues without requiring human review of its actions. The agent ran with broad privileges and accepted prompts directly from issue titles submitted by anyone. An attacker could craft a malicious issue title containing instructions that the AI would follow, allowing them to inject commands that the system would execute. This is a failure to gate AI decision-making with human review and a failure to isolate AI systems from untrusted input.

The compromise created a path to steal publishing credentials and inject malicious code into software packages downloaded by millions of developers. An attacker combined prompt injection with a GitHub Actions cache poisoning technique to gain access to the credentials needed to publish unauthorized updates to NPM, VS Code Marketplace, and OpenVSX. Catching this would have required either restricting the AI agent's capabilities, requiring human approval before it took actions with security consequences, or treating all user-submitted GitHub issue content as untrusted.

It is not established that the vulnerability was exploited to publish malicious updates before it was fixed, though evidence suggests someone may have attempted to do so.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, contained a critical security vulnerability from December 21, 2025 to February 9, 2026. The Cline team deployed an AI agent to automatically triage GitHub issues, but this agent ran with broad privileges and accepted prompts directly from issue titles. A researcher named Adnan Khan discovered that attackers could craft malicious issue titles to inject prompts that tricked the AI into running arbitrary code. By exploiting this vulnerability along with a GitHub Actions cache poisoning technique, an attacker could steal publishing credentials and push malicious updates to millions of developers across VS Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM.

Khan attempted to report the vulnerability through multiple channels starting January 1st but received no response from Cline's team. After going public on February 9th, Cline fixed the issue within an hour and confirmed they had rotated credentials and removed the vulnerable workflows. Evidence suggests someone may have attempted to exploit the vulnerability, though no malicious updates were confirmed. Cline now advises users to disable auto-updates and avoid updating until the team confirms no credentials were compromised.
